title: Merge Sort, Step by Step
excerpt: A complete trace of merge sort on a seven-element array: every split, every merge, and the execution order that almost everyone gets wrong the first time.
seoTitle: Merge Sort Step by Step: Full Trace, Recursion Order and the Merge
seoDescription: Merge sort traced completely on a 7-element array: every split, the exact depth-first call order, one merge shown pointer by pointer, and flowcharts of both halves.

content.text: Merge sort rests on two facts, both of them obvious on their own.
First: an array with one element is already sorted. Second: two sorted arrays can be combined into one sorted array in a single pass, by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two front values.

Put those together and you have the algorithm. Split the array until every piece has one element, which makes them all sorted by definition, then merge pairs back together until there is one array left.
Everything below traces this array all the way through:
Each call finds the midpoint and splits there. Seven elements split into three and four, then those split again, and so on until every piece has one element.
Notice the splitting never looks at the values. It only looks at the length. That is why merge sort takes the same time on sorted, reversed and random input: the shape of this tree depends only on n.
The tree is
log₂ n
levels deep, because each level halves the size. Seven elements gives three levels of splitting.

body.text: Step 2: the order things actually happen

content.text: This is the part that trips people up, so it is worth being precise. Merge sort does
not

split everything into single elements and then merge everything back. It is depth-first: it fully finishes the entire left half, all the way down and all the way back up, before it even looks at the right half.
Here is every call, in the exact order it happens, with indentation showing recursion depth.

body.code:
1  mergeSort([38,27,43,3,9,82,10])  ->  split into [38,27,43] and [3,9,82,10]
 2    mergeSort([38,27,43])          ->  split into [38] and [27,43]
 3      mergeSort([38])              ->  base case, return [38]
 4      mergeSort([27,43])           ->  split into [27] and [43]
 5        mergeSort([27])            ->  base case, return [27]
 6        mergeSort([43])            ->  base case, return [43]
 7      merge([27], [43])            ->  [27,43]
 8    merge([38], [27,43])           ->  [27,38,43]      <- left half done
 9    mergeSort([3,9,82,10])         ->  split into [3,9] and [82,10]
10      mergeSort([3,9])             ->  split into [3] and [9]
11        mergeSort([3])             ->  base case, return [3]
12        mergeSort([9])             ->  base case, return [9]
13      merge([3], [9])              ->  [3,9]
14      mergeSort([82,10])           ->  split into [82] and [10]
15        mergeSort([82])            ->  base case, return [82]
16        mergeSort([10])            ->  base case, return [10]
17      merge([82], [10])            ->  [10,82]
18    merge([3,9], [10,82])          ->  [3,9,10,82]     <- right half done
19  merge([27,38,43], [3,9,10,82])   ->  [3,9,10,27,38,43,82]

content.text: Look at step 7. A merge happens at step 7, before the right half of the original array has been touched at all:
mergeSort([3,9,82,10])
does not begin until step 9.
That is what "depth-first" means here. The call at step 2 cannot return until steps 3 through 8 have all completed, and the call at step 1 cannot merge until both step 8 and step 18 have returned.
Nineteen steps in total: 7 base cases, 6 merges, and 6 splits. In general there are n leaves, n-1 merges, and n-1 splits.
At any moment during the run, the call stack holds one path from the root down to wherever you currently are. At step 5, for instance, the stack looks like this, most recent call last:

body.code:
mergeSort([38,27,43,3,9,82,10])     waiting on its left half
  mergeSort([38,27,43])             waiting on its left half
    mergeSort([27,43])              waiting on its left half
      mergeSort([27])               running now, returns immediately

content.text: Every frame below the top is parked, holding a local variable for its left result and waiting. That is where the sorted halves live between the split and the merge: not in some global structure, but in the local variables of paused function calls, one per level. Since the tree is log n deep, so is the stack.
Step through the visualizer below and watch the highlighted range narrow as it descends, then widen again as merges complete. The highlighted region is exactly the call at the top of the stack.
The merge is where the actual sorting happens. Take step 19, the final merge of
and
. Both inputs are already sorted, which is the only thing that makes this work.
Keep a pointer at the front of each side, compare the two values under the pointers, take the smaller, and advance that pointer. Repeat.

Seven elements, six comparisons, one pass. The loop ends as soon as either side runs out, and whatever is left on the other side is copied across wholesale, because it is already sorted and already larger than everything emitted so far.

body.text: The one line that decides stability

content.text: When the two front values are equal, which side do you take from?
Take from the
left

. The left half came earlier in the original array, so taking it first preserves the original relative order of equal elements, which is the definition of a stable sort. In code that is the difference between
left[i] <= right[j]
and
left[i] < right[j]

With plain numbers you cannot tell the difference, because two equal numbers are indistinguishable. Sort records with equal keys and it matters a great deal, which is why that comparison operator is worth being deliberate about.
A flowchart cannot express "call yourself", so what follows is the shape of a
single call
, with the two recursive steps shown as ordinary boxes. Click any box with a dot to see what it is for.
The base case is the exit that stops the recursion, and without it, splitting would continue forever on empty arrays.
And here is the merge step, which does have a genuine loop:

The dashed copper arrows are the loop: both branches of the comparison rejoin and go back to the "are both sides non-empty" test. When that test fails, at most one of the two drain steps has anything left to do.

body.text: Why it is n log n

content.text: Count the work per level rather than per call. At every level of the tree, the merges together touch each of the n elements exactly once, so each level costs O(n). There are log₂ n levels. Multiply and you get O(n log n).
For the example: level 1 merges 7 elements in total, level 2 merges 7, level 3 merges 6. Roughly n per level, three levels.

No input changes this, because the split is positional. That is both merge sort's guarantee and its limitation: it cannot exploit input that is already partly sorted, which is exactly the gap Timsort fills by detecting existing runs before it starts.

rows: O(n log n) in all three
Yes, when ties take from the left
No, unless run detection is added

body.text: Where merge sort is the right answer

content.text: External sorting

. If the data does not fit in memory, merge sort still works: sort chunks that do fit, write them to disk, then merge the sorted files by streaming them. The merge only ever needs the front of each run, so it can combine files far larger than RAM.
Linked lists
. Merging a linked list needs no extra memory at all, since it is just relinking. Quick sort is awkward on lists because it depends on indexing.
When the worst case matters, quick sort is usually faster but can degrade to O(n²), and merge sort cannot.
It is also the basis of
Timsort
, the default sort in Python, Java for objects, Android, V8 and Swift.

questions.prompt: In the trace, merge([27],[43]) happens at step 7. What has NOT happened yet at that point?

options.label: The right half [3,9,82,10] has not been touched at all
The array has not been split yet
The base cases have not been reached

questions.prompt: Where are the sorted halves stored between a split and its merge?

options.label: In the local variables of paused function calls, one per level of the stack
In a single global buffer shared by all calls
They are recomputed from scratch at merge time

questions.prompt: Why is merge sort's cost identical on sorted and reversed input?

options.label: The split is positional and never inspects the values, so the tree shape depends only on n
Because it always does exactly n^2/2 comparisons
It is not; sorted input is much faster

questions.prompt: The merge loop exits when one side empties. Why can the rest of the other side simply be copied?

options.label: It is already sorted and every value in it is larger than everything already emitted
Because the remaining values are always equal
It cannot; it must be merged element by element
